Subject: Technical deep dive — latency & throughput SLOs (Acme Analytics)

Thanks for the call this morning — great to meet the Acme team. Below is a short recap of what we heard, what we proposed, and next steps. Please flag anything I missed.

High-level pain points (from Samir + Lina):
- Unpredictable tail latency during peak business hours (reporting spikes around 3–4 PM ET)
- Cost per inference at scale is rising; need predictable unit economics
- Concern about cold-start behavior for episodic workloads and large context windows

Goals / target SLOs discussed:
- P95 latency <= 250ms for typical short queries (<= 64 tokens)
- P99 latency target <= 600ms for mixed-length requests (avg 150 tokens)
- Sustained throughput goal: 200 req/s with 512-token sequences during peak
- Support context window up to 2048 tokens for long-form analysis use cases

Model + deployment constraints:
- Preference for a quantized 7B–13B model family that supports 2048 context window and performs well on NVidia A10/A100 class GPUs
- Strong desire for private VPC deployment and audit logging (SOC2/compliance sensitive)

Initial deployment topology we discussed:
- Dedicated GPU pool in us-west (to reduce cross-region latency) with autoscale floor to meet 200 req/s
- Prefix/KV caching for short conversational hits to reduce token cost and tail latency
- Canary rollout for model version changes and a fast fallback policy to a smaller model variant if latency spikes

Attachments I uploaded for your review: redwood-slo-template.xlsx, proposed-topology-diagram.png (high level).

Next steps (action owners):
- Acme: confirm peak-hour windows and share a sample trace/log (Samir) — due EOD Tue 2027-04-06
- Redwood SE: provide cold-start and warm-up behavior, recommended model configs and batch sizing (Connor) — deliver by Mon 2027-04-05
- Redwood AE: send proposal/estimate and reserve a technical workshop to validate SLOs (Neha/Marissa)

Happy to set up a 90-minute deep-dive (hands-on with your sample traces) if that helps. Proposed window: week of Apr 12.

Thanks,

Hi Samir — quick technical notes based on your questions and the goals Marissa captured. High-level answers first, details below.

Summary answers:
- Cold-start: model cold-start (GPU model weight load) can range from ~600ms–1.2s depending on model size and sharding; for 13B it's toward the higher end if loading from scratch. We recommend an autoscale floor with pre-warmed workers for predictable tail latency.
- Cache eviction: Redwood's KV/prefix cache uses LRU with hot-key pinning options. For long interactive sessions we can pin the session's KV to a worker pool to avoid eviction during bursts (configurable per-customer).
- SOC2/compliance: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II compliant; I'll share the access link via secure portal. For private VPC deployments we provide HSM/KMS integrations and audit log exports.

Technical details:
- Warm vs cold: In Dedicated mode we support a pre-warm policy (reserve a minimal number of pods with model weights resident). Cold model load (from disk) is the dominant factor; in practice with NVMe + A10/A100 GPUs we see: 7B quantized ~450–700ms, 13B quantized ~800–1200ms to first token.
- Batching & throughput: For 512-token sequences, target batch sizes of 8–16 give good GPU utilization depending on model architecture and kernel selection. Continuous batching reduces per-token cost but increases median latency; we tune to meet P95 constraints.
- KV cache and TTLs: default TTL 30m; can set session pinning for critical users. Cache eviction is LRU with metrics exposed in the console for hit/miss rates.
- Network & topology: recommend colocating the inference pool in us-west2 and keeping the frontend load-balancers in the same region to avoid cross-region hops; provide private peering for VPC deployments and limit egress.

Attachments: I uploaded a quick SLO-calculations.csv with example compute and cost assumptions for 200 req/s sustained at different token distributions. Also included a short note on model recommendations (LLaMA-2-13B Quant-8, LLaMA-2-7B Quant-4 as fallback).

If helpful, we can run a small spike test (2–4 hours) on a dedicated pool to validate P95 numbers against a representative traffic trace. That normally takes 48–72 hours to schedule for reserved capacity.
